passage_title: What the Hands Know
passage:
[1] The bell over the door of Ostrowski Clock & Watch had a crack in it, so it did not ring so much as clatter, and by the second week of June Lena had stopped hearing it at all. She came in at nine, hung her bag on the hook behind the counter, and waited for her grandfather to look up from the bench. Some mornings he did. Some mornings he only lifted two fingers from the loupe, which meant the same thing.

[2] Her mother had presented the arrangement as a favor to Lena. "You'll learn something," she had said, in the voice she used for dentist appointments. Lena had understood, without anyone saying so, that the favor ran the other way. Her grandfather had lived alone above the shop since March. The apartment had one chair at the kitchen table now; the other had been moved, for reasons no one explained, to the landing.

[3] The work itself was smaller than she expected. Most of what came through the door was batteries. A woman would slide a wristwatch across the glass, and Lena would pry off the back with a tool like a tiny crowbar, and the whole transaction took four minutes. Her grandfather did not do batteries anymore. He sat at the back bench under the lamp with the green shade, and the things he opened had names she learned slowly: mainspring, escapement, balance wheel. He worked with tweezers whose tips were finer than the lead in a pencil.

[4] It was the tweezers she noticed first. On the third Tuesday he was fitting a hairspring, a coil of blued steel no wider than an eyelash, into a pocket watch that had belonged to somebody's great-uncle. She was sweeping. She saw the tweezers approach the watch, pause a quarter inch above it, and hold there, trembling very slightly, the way the surface of a glass of water trembles when a truck goes by outside. Then he set the tweezers down, flexed his hand twice under the bench where he must have thought she couldn't see, and picked them up again.

[5] "Hand me the brass one," he said, without turning. She handed him the brass one. He did not need it; it lay untouched beside the lamp for the rest of the afternoon.

[6] After that she began to keep a kind of ledger in her head. Monday: the hairspring again, and again the pause. Wednesday: he asked her to read him the serial number off a movement, though the numbers were engraved a half inch from his nose and she had seen him read the date off a penny across the room. Thursday: a customer, an impatient man in a suit, wanted his watch regulated while he waited, and her grandfather said the machine was booked and he'd have to leave it. There was no machine. There was a small brass timing stand that had never, to her knowledge, been booked by anyone.

[7] She did not mention any of this to her mother. When her mother called on Sunday and asked how it was going, Lena said, "Fine. He's teaching me the escapement," which was true, and let the rest of the sentence stay where it was.

[8] The following week she came in early, before nine, and rearranged the bench. She did it quickly, the way you pull off a bandage. The lamp came six inches closer to the vise. The good tweezers went into the front slot of the tray, where a hand would find them first without having to choose. She took the magnifying visor from the shelf where it had been gathering dust since before her time and set it on the bench, not in the center, where it would look like a suggestion, but off to the side near the parts drawers, where it might have been left by accident. Then she went and stood behind the counter and pretended to read the battery catalog.

[9] He came down at nine. He stood in front of the bench for a while with his coat still on. She turned a page. She heard the stool scrape, and the lamp's chain, and then a long nothing that she did not dare look up into. When she finally did, the visor was on his head, pushed up on his forehead like a welder's mask, and he was bent over the great-uncle's watch, and the hairspring was going in.

[10] "The bell," he said, later, while she was closing out the register. "It's cracked. Been cracked for years." He did not look at her when he said it. "Your grandmother always said she'd get it fixed, and I always said I'd do it myself." He took a slow breath through his nose. "You could order one. If you wanted. There's a catalog somewhere."

[11] Lena said she would look. Then she reached under the counter for the catalog, which was not, in fact, somewhere; it was right there, where it had always been, and she had read it twice.

passage_title: Fine-Free Libraries: Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] In 2019 the public library system of a mid-sized river city became one of several dozen in the country to stop charging daily fines for overdue books. The decision was not a gesture. It followed an internal audit that found fines produced barely one percent of the system's operating revenue while consuming roughly the same share of staff time to collect, dispute, and waive. On the numbers alone, the fines were a wash. What the audit could not show, and what the following three years did, was what the fines had been costing in patrons.

[2] Before the change, about 11,000 cardholders, one in nine, carried a balance high enough to block borrowing. Those blocked accounts were not distributed evenly. In the two branches serving the city's lowest-income neighborhoods, the blocked share was nearly one in four. A fine of a few dollars is a nuisance in one household and a reason to stop coming in another, and the children in the second household stop coming too, because their cards are tied to their parents'.

[3] When the fines were forgiven and the daily charge abolished, those accounts were unlocked in a single day. Over the following eighteen months, new card registrations rose 15 percent systemwide and 28 percent at the two branches with the highest blocked rates. Circulation at those branches rose by a fifth, and staff, no longer collecting and disputing small balances, reported spending more of their desk hours on reference questions and children's programs. Critics predicted that without a penalty, materials would simply never come back. That did not happen. The system kept a replacement charge for items more than sixty days overdue, and the proportion of items eventually returned, 96 percent before the change, settled at 95 percent after it.

[4] The lesson is not complicated. Fines were doing almost nothing to bring books back and a great deal to keep people out. A library's mission is not to maximize the return rate of its inventory; it is to be used, and by the people who have the fewest other options. A policy that quietly turned away a quarter of the patrons in the neighborhoods that needed the building most was not a small administrative matter. Removing it was the most consequential thing the system did that decade, and it cost, in net terms, nothing.

Passage B

[1] The case for fine-free libraries rests on a before-and-after comparison, and before-and-after comparisons are where good intentions go to be flattered. Yes, registrations rose after the river city forgave its fines. Registrations also rose in the neighboring county, which kept its fines, and by a similar margin, because 2019 through 2021 were years when libraries everywhere expanded digital lending, extended weekend hours, and ran registration drives in schools. The river city did all three. Attributing the gain to the fine policy is not analysis; it is choosing the explanation one hoped to find.

[2] The claim that fines "kept people out" also deserves more scrutiny than it usually gets. Blocked accounts are real, but an account blocked for a balance does not mean a person who wanted to borrow and could not. Many were dormant: cards issued years earlier, never renewed, carrying a balance from a book long since replaced. Counting them as excluded patrons inflates the injury. Surveys of nonusers in the same neighborhoods, taken both before and after the change, consistently ranked fines well below transportation, hours, and simple lack of awareness as reasons for not visiting.

[3] None of this means daily fines are good policy. The audit's own finding, that they cost about as much to administer as they raised, is a sufficient reason to drop them. But it is a modest, budgetary reason, and dressing it in the language of justice does something unhelpful: it lets a system claim a victory over inequity while the actual barriers go unaddressed. The two low-income branches in the river city still close at six on weekdays. Neither is on a bus line that runs after seven. A patron who could not get to the building in 2018 still cannot.

[4] There is also a cost that the fine-free accounting leaves out. The 95 percent return rate is reassuring as an average, but the items that do not come back are not a random sample; they are disproportionately new and popular titles, which now spend longer on the "checked out" shelf of the catalog than they did. The library did not lose money. It lost, a little, the thing it exists to provide: the book being on the shelf when the next person comes for it. Whether that trade was worth making is a fair question. It should at least be asked as one.

passage:
[1] The phrase "silent film" is one of those labels that describes an absence and gets the absence wrong. The films were silent; the theaters were not. From the first storefront nickelodeons of the early twentieth century to the grand picture palaces of the late 1920s, almost no commercial screening in an American city took place without live music, and the person supplying it, at a piano, an organ, or the podium of a small orchestra, had a job that has no exact equivalent in any later art form.

[2] Consider what the job required. A neighborhood pianist might see four different programs a week, each running ninety minutes or more, and would typically play the first showing of each without having seen the film. There was no score. There was, at best, a "cue sheet" mailed out by the distributor: a list of scene descriptions paired with suggested pieces, so that a title card reading "The Storm Breaks" might be matched to a well-known overture, and a lovers' parting to a popular ballad. The suggestions were just that. Whether the theater owned the sheet music, whether the pianist could play it, whether the reel had been cut by a local censor so that the storm was now twenty seconds shorter: none of this was the distributor's concern.

[3] So the accompanist improvised, and the improvisation was the craft. Published anthologies of "photoplay music" appeared by the 1910s, organized not by composer but by situation: "Hurry (for chases)," "Misterioso (for sinister approach)," "Agitato (for storms, riots, battles)," "Pathetic (for grief)." A competent player learned dozens of these short pieces and, more importantly, learned to move between them without a seam, stretching an eight-bar phrase to sixteen when a chase ran long and collapsing a love theme to a single cadence when the director cut away early. The music followed the picture, second by second, and the person doing the following was making decisions faster than any composer at a desk ever had to.

[4] Not everyone approved. Trade journals of the period are full of complaints from critics and studio executives about accompanists who played too loudly, played the wrong mood, or, most damningly, played the same handful of pieces for every film regardless of content. One columnist described sitting through a funeral scene set to a foxtrot because the pianist had run out of slow music. The studios' response, by the mid-1920s, was to commission original scores for their most expensive productions and distribute them with the prints, along with instructions that they be played as written. The scores traveled well to the palaces, which had orchestras and rehearsal time. They traveled poorly to everywhere else.

[5] It is tempting to read this history as a story of standardization defeating chaos, of the composed score finally bringing order to a practice that had been, at its worst, a foxtrot at a funeral. The musicologist Delphine Achterberg has argued for a different reading. "The accompanist's music was not a rough draft of the film score," she writes. "It was a separate art, performed in the same room as the film, and it answered to the audience in front of it rather than to the print in the can." Her point is that the improvising pianist could do something no distributed score could: respond to the particular room. If a crowd laughed at a scene the director had meant to be tense, the pianist could go with the laugh. If a local reel was missing a scene, the music simply did not include it. The composed score, played as written, was faithful to the film and deaf to the theater.

[6] The end came quickly. Synchronized sound arrived commercially in 1927, and within four years the vast majority of American theaters had been wired for it. Estimates vary, but somewhere in the range of twenty thousand theater musicians lost their positions in that span, a displacement that the musicians' unions fought and lost. The picture palaces kept their organs for a few more years as a novelty for intermissions; the neighborhood houses simply sold the piano.

[7] What was lost is hard to describe, because it was never recorded. A performance that existed only in a specific room on a specific night, adjusted to a specific audience, left nothing behind except the cue sheets, the anthologies, and the complaints. Historians reconstructing the practice work from those fragments the way one might reconstruct a cuisine from its shopping lists. The food itself is gone. But the lists are enough to make clear that "silent film" was, for the people who actually sat in the dark and watched it, a misnomer from the first frame to the last.

[1] The phrase "silent film" is one of those labels that describes an absence and gets the absence wrong. The films were silent; the theaters were not. From the first storefront nickelodeons of the early twentieth century to the grand picture palaces of the late 1920s, almost no commercial screening in an American city took place without live music, and the person supplying it, at a piano, an organ, or the podium of a small orchestra, had a job that has no exact equivalent in any later art form.

[2] Consider what the job required. A neighborhood pianist might see four different programs a week, each running ninety minutes or more, and would typically play the first showing of each without having seen the film. There was no score. There was, at best, a "cue sheet" mailed out by the distributor: a list of scene descriptions paired with suggested pieces, so that a title card reading "The Storm Breaks" might be matched to a well-known overture, and a lovers' parting to a popular ballad. The suggestions were just that. Whether the theater owned the sheet music, whether the pianist could play it, whether the reel had been cut by a local censor so that the storm was now twenty seconds shorter: none of this was the distributor's concern.

[3] So the accompanist improvised, and the improvisation was the craft. Published anthologies of "photoplay music" appeared by the 1910s, organized not by composer but by situation: "Hurry (for chases)," "Misterioso (for sinister approach)," "Agitato (for storms, riots, battles)," "Pathetic (for grief)." A competent player learned dozens of these short pieces and, more importantly, learned to move between them without a seam, stretching an eight-bar phrase to sixteen when a chase ran long and collapsing a love theme to a single cadence when the director cut away early. The music followed the picture, second by second, and the person doing the following was making decisions faster than any composer at a desk ever had to.

[4] Not everyone approved. Trade journals of the period are full of complaints from critics and studio executives about accompanists who played too loudly, played the wrong mood, or, most damningly, played the same handful of pieces for every film regardless of content. One columnist described sitting through a funeral scene set to a foxtrot because the pianist had run out of slow music. The studios' response, by the mid-1920s, was to commission original scores for their most expensive productions and distribute them with the prints, along with instructions that they be played as written. The scores traveled well to the palaces, which had orchestras and rehearsal time. They traveled poorly to everywhere else.

[5] It is tempting to read this history as a story of standardization defeating chaos, of the composed score finally bringing order to a practice that had been, at its worst, a foxtrot at a funeral. The musicologist Delphine Achterberg has argued for a different reading. "The accompanist's music was not a rough draft of the film score," she writes. "It was a separate art, performed in the same room as the film, and it answered to the audience in front of it rather than to the print in the can." Her point is that the improvising pianist could do something no distributed score could: respond to the particular room. If a crowd laughed at a scene the director had meant to be tense, the pianist could go with the laugh. If a local reel was missing a scene, the music simply did not include it. The composed score, played as written, was faithful to the film and deaf to the theater.

[6] The end came quickly. Synchronized sound arrived commercially in 1927, and within four years the vast majority of American theaters had been wired for it. Estimates vary, but somewhere in the range of twenty thousand theater musicians lost their positions in that span, a displacement that the musicians' unions fought and lost. The picture palaces kept their organs for a few more years as a novelty for intermissions; the neighborhood houses simply sold the piano.

[7] What was lost is hard to describe, because it was never recorded. A performance that existed only in a specific room on a specific night, adjusted to a specific audience, left nothing behind except the cue sheets, the anthologies, and the complaints. Historians reconstructing the practice work from those fragments the way one might reconstruct a cuisine from its shopping lists. The food itself is gone. passage_title: Warm Sand, Cool Sand: Temperature and the Sex of Sea Turtles
passage:
[1] A female loggerhead sea turtle hauls herself onto a beach at night, digs a flask-shaped chamber in the sand with her hind flippers, deposits around a hundred leathery eggs, covers them, and returns to the sea. She will not see the nest again. Everything that happens next, how fast the embryos develop, how many survive, and, remarkably, whether they become male or female, is decided by the sand.

[2] In humans and most other mammals, sex is fixed at fertilization by the chromosomes an embryo inherits. Sea turtles, along with all crocodilians and many lizards, do something different. Their embryos carry no sex chromosomes at all. Instead, sex is set during a window in the middle third of incubation by the temperature of the nest, a mechanism biologists call temperature-dependent sex determination, or TSD. For sea turtles the relationship runs in one direction: cooler nests produce mostly males, warmer nests produce mostly females. The temperature at which a clutch would split evenly is called the pivotal temperature, and for most loggerhead populations it lies close to 29 degrees Celsius.

[3] The transition is not gradual across the whole range of survivable temperatures. It is steep. A nest held a degree and a half below pivotal will yield almost entirely males; a nest a degree and a half above will yield almost entirely females. Within the narrow band around pivotal, often less than two degrees wide, small differences in shade, sand color, depth, and rainfall can swing a clutch from one sex to the other. Because temperature also governs the speed of development, warmer nests hatch sooner, and a field biologist who records only the number of days between laying and emergence can estimate, with fair accuracy, what the sex ratio of the emerged hatchlings is likely to be.

[4] The table below summarizes incubation results from a set of experimental nests in which eggs from a single population were held at constant temperatures.

Nest temperature (°C) | Incubation period (days) | Female hatchlings (%)
27.0 | 68 | 6
28.0 | 62 | 21
29.0 | 57 | 51
30.0 | 52 | 83
31.0 | 48 | 97
32.5 | 45 | 100

[5] Two features of the table matter for what follows. First, the incubation period shortens steadily as temperature rises, by roughly five or six days per degree in the middle of the range. Second, the proportion of females moves from a small minority to nearly all within a span of about three degrees. A nest that emerges after 60 days and a nest that emerges after 50 days, on the same beach in the same season, have very likely produced hatchlings of predominantly different sexes.

[6] Why a mechanism like this should have evolved is still debated. One long-standing hypothesis holds that TSD lets each sex be produced under the conditions that suit it best; that, for instance, females emerging from warm nests hatch larger or earlier and gain some lifelong advantage from it. Evidence for that advantage in sea turtles specifically has been hard to come by, in part because a loggerhead may take thirty years to mature and its reproductive success cannot be tracked from the nest. A less flattering possibility is that TSD is simply an ancestral condition that reptiles have retained because, until recently, nothing much punished it.

[7] What has changed is the sand. Nesting beaches in several regions have warmed by more than a degree over the past half century, and at some of them the recorded hatchling sex ratios are now heavily female; in a few surveyed rookeries, above nine females to one male among recent cohorts. A population can tolerate a female skew for a time, since one male can fertilize the eggs of many females. But the skew has a limit, and beyond a certain temperature the question of sex becomes moot: embryos held above roughly 33 to 34 degrees for extended periods die regardless.

[8] Conservation programs have responded with measures that sound modest and are not. Shade cloth stretched over nesting areas can lower sand temperature by one to two degrees, enough to move a clutch across pivotal. Relocating clutches to cooler, deeper, or more shaded stretches of beach does the same, though handling eggs carries its own risks. At a few sites, managers have begun watering nests during the hottest weeks. Each of these interventions requires knowing, beach by beach, where the local pivotal temperature sits and how far above it the sand has drifted, which is why the unglamorous work of burying thermometers in nests, and counting the days until the hatchlings emerge, has become some of the most consequential fieldwork in marine conservation.

passage:
[1] A female loggerhead sea turtle hauls herself onto a beach at night, digs a flask-shaped chamber in the sand with her hind flippers, deposits around a hundred leathery eggs, covers them, and returns to the sea. She will not see the nest again. Everything that happens next, how fast the embryos develop, how many survive, and, remarkably, whether they become male or female, is decided by the sand.

[2] In humans and most other mammals, sex is fixed at fertilization by the chromosomes an embryo inherits. Sea turtles, along with all crocodilians and many lizards, do something different. Their embryos carry no sex chromosomes at all. Instead, sex is set during a window in the middle third of incubation by the temperature of the nest, a mechanism biologists call temperature-dependent sex determination, or TSD. For sea turtles the relationship runs in one direction: cooler nests produce mostly males, warmer nests produce mostly females. The temperature at which a clutch would split evenly is called the pivotal temperature, and for most loggerhead populations it lies close to 29 degrees Celsius.

[3] The transition is not gradual across the whole range of survivable temperatures. It is steep. A nest held a degree and a half below pivotal will yield almost entirely males; a nest a degree and a half above will yield almost entirely females. Within the narrow band around pivotal, often less than two degrees wide, small differences in shade, sand color, depth, and rainfall can swing a clutch from one sex to the other. Because temperature also governs the speed of development, warmer nests hatch sooner, and a field biologist who records only the number of days between laying and emergence can estimate, with fair accuracy, what the sex ratio of the emerged hatchlings is likely to be.

[4] The table below summarizes incubation results from a set of experimental nests in which eggs from a single population were held at constant temperatures.

Nest temperature (°C) | Incubation period (days) | Female hatchlings (%)
27.0 | 68 | 6
28.0 | 62 | 21
29.0 | 57 | 51
30.0 | 52 | 83
31.0 | 48 | 97
32.5 | 45 | 100

[5] Two features of the table matter for what follows. First, the incubation period shortens steadily as temperature rises, by roughly five or six days per degree in the middle of the range. Second, the proportion of females moves from a small minority to nearly all within a span of about three degrees. A nest that emerges after 60 days and a nest that emerges after 50 days, on the same beach in the same season, have very likely produced hatchlings of predominantly different sexes.

[6] Why a mechanism like this should have evolved is still debated. One long-standing hypothesis holds that TSD lets each sex be produced under the conditions that suit it best; that, for instance, females emerging from warm nests hatch larger or earlier and gain some lifelong advantage from it. Evidence for that advantage in sea turtles specifically has been hard to come by, in part because a loggerhead may take thirty years to mature and its reproductive success cannot be tracked from the nest. A less flattering possibility is that TSD is simply an ancestral condition that reptiles have retained because, until recently, nothing much punished it.

[7] What has changed is the sand. Nesting beaches in several regions have warmed by more than a degree over the past half century, and at some of them the recorded hatchling sex ratios are now heavily female; in a few surveyed rookeries, above nine females to one male among recent cohorts.
